scenarios.scenario: Engineers kick off long agent runs and switch to other windows. They want an OS desktop alert the moment the run is blocked waiting for an approval or for input, without anyone watching the terminal.

key.primary: Notification hook, with matchers for notification types such as permission_prompt and idle_prompt, whose command fires the OS notifier
key.rejected_alternative: A Stop hook that sends the alert when Claude finishes responding
key.rejection_reason: Stop fires only when Claude ends its turn. A session blocked mid-turn on a permission prompt has not stopped, so a Stop-based alert never fires at the moment attention is actually needed. Notification is the documented event for permission prompts and idle waiting, and the hooks guide's first walkthrough is exactly this desktop-alert use case.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the notifier is a pure side-effect command fired on the Notification event); nothing crosses back into the conversation: the event supports no decision control, and even blocking stderr is shown to the user only, never to Claude
key.lifecycle: Notification event fires whenever Claude Code sends a notification; the matcher selects types like permission_prompt or idle_prompt
key.failure_mode: Notification hook output and exit code are ignored by design, so a broken notifier command fails completely silently: no alert and no surfaced error.

sheets.primary: A Notification hook in settings.json that runs a small OS-notifier command (PowerShell toast on Windows, terminal-notifier or osascript on macOS, notify-send on Linux) using the message and session details supplied on stdin. The command is the whole implementation; no model involvement at all.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A Stop hook, which is the usual notify-me choice but fires when the turn ends rather than when the run is blocked mid-turn waiting on a person, so it answers a different question.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. It decides when a notification event occurs and launches the command; the model neither knows nor influences whether an alert was raised.
sheets.context_boundary: The notifier runs out of process and its output is not needed by the agent, so nothing meaningful crosses back into the context window. The blocked session stays parked exactly where it was.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered each time the CLI emits a notification event, which covers a pending permission prompt and a prolonged idle wait for input. It stops when the session ends or when the hook entry is removed.
sheets.failure_mode: Purely advisory, and it fails silently open: if the notifier binary is absent, if the run is over SSH, inside a container, in WSL, or under a headless CI user, no toast appears and the run simply sits blocked with nobody informed. Notification storms during a chatty session also train people to ignore it.
sheets.version_caveat: This depends on a Notification hook event existing in the installed version and on the idle-wait threshold that triggers it. I cannot confirm from model knowledge alone either the exact event name spelling or the idle timeout value, so both should be verified against the running release before promising the alert covers the input-wait case as well as the approval case.

sheets.primary: A Notification hook in ~/.claude/settings.json (or shipped fleet-wide as a plugin) with matcher "permission_prompt", running the platform notifier: osascript display notification on macOS, notify-send on Linux, a PowerShell message box or toast on Windows. Add a second entry with matcher "idle_prompt" if 'Claude is done and waiting for your next prompt' should also alert.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that fires a notification before every tool call. It would alert continuously rather than only when the run is actually blocked, since it cannot tell which calls will prompt and which are auto-approved.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness fires the event and runs the command; the model has no part in it and cannot suppress or trigger the alert.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs as a subprocess in the developer's own OS session, outside the model's context window: the notification event JSON goes in on stdin and nothing comes back into the conversation. Notification is one of the events where exit code 2 cannot block anything, so the hook is purely a side effect.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires each time Claude Code emits a notification of the matched type, for the life of every session once the hook is in user settings. It stops when the hook entry is removed or hooks are disabled, and it never fires for a run that is not actually waiting.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory: it can raise the alert but cannot make anyone respond, and delivery failures are silent. On macOS osascript routes through Script Editor, which silently drops notifications until that app is granted notification permission once, and in an SSH session or container there is often no desktop notification bus at all, so notify-send just errors while the run stays blocked unseen.
sheets.version_caveat: The permission_prompt and idle_prompt matchers are generally available. The agent_needs_input and agent_completed matchers, which cover background sessions, require Claude Code v2.1.198 or later and fire only while agent view is open, so they are not a substitute for the terminal-session case.

sheets.primary: A Notification hook in each engineer's user-level ~/.claude/settings.json, with a permission_prompt matcher wired to an OS notifier command, plus separate matchers for idle_prompt and, for background runs, agent_needs_input.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A Stop hook. It fires when the main agent has finished responding, which is the wrong moment: a run blocked mid-turn on an approval has not stopped, so the alert would arrive late or not at all.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code raises the notification event and runs the hook command; the model neither decides that a notification happens nor sees that one was sent.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs out of process and receives message, title and notification_type on stdin. The desktop alert lives entirely outside the context window; nothing crosses back into the conversation except an optional systemMessage.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires each time Claude Code emits a notification whose type matches, for every session on that machine while the settings entry exists. It stops applying when the entry is removed, or when the notification type simply does not fire, such as the background-session types outside agent view.
sheets.failure_mode: Purely advisory: notification hooks cannot block or modify notifications, so a missing, slow or misconfigured notifier silently drops the alert and the run sits blocked with nobody informed. Coverage is also partial: agent_needs_input and agent_completed fire only while agent view is open in a terminal, so an engineer who closed it gets nothing for background sessions.
sheets.version_caveat: The agent_needs_input and agent_completed notification types require Claude Code v2.1.198 or later; permission_prompt and idle_prompt carry no version gate. There is no plan restriction, but desktop delivery depends on an OS notifier being present on each machine.

sheets.primary: A Notification hook, command handler, in each engineer's ~/.claude/settings.json, invoking the platform notifier (osascript, notify-send, or a PowerShell toast) with the matcher scoped to permission_prompt and idle_prompt so it fires exactly when the run is blocked. An empty matcher fires on every notification type if broader coverage is wanted.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook on all tools, which fires on every tool call whether or not a prompt will actually appear, so it cannot tell blocked from proceeding and buries the engineer in false alerts.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns firing: Claude Code emits the Notification event when it is waiting on the human, and the handler is only responsible for delivering the alert to the desktop.
sheets.context_boundary: The handler is a separate process outside the session context; it receives message, optional title and notification_type on stdin, and nothing it produces returns to the model, since the alert is a pure side effect aimed at the human.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs each time Claude Code emits a notification of a matching type, for the life of every session on that machine, and stops applying when the user settings entry is removed or hooks are disabled.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Notification hooks cannot block or modify anything, exit 2 only shows stderr to the user, and a silently failing notifier (the documented macOS Script Editor permission case) leaves the engineer with no alert and no error, so the alert path itself needs a live test.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate applies to permission_prompt or idle_prompt, which is the pair this need requires. The agent_needs_input and agent_completed matchers require Claude Code v2.1.198 or later and additionally only fire while agent view is open, so they are the wrong choice for a terminal run.

scenarios.scenario: We run the agent in a fully auto-approved configuration for speed, but any git push must still halt and wait for a human to explicitly confirm, every single time, no matter what approval configuration the session is running under.

key.primary: A permissions ask rule such as Bash(git push *), which forces a confirmation prompt on every matching call
key.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask" for git push commands
key.rejection_reason: bypassPermissions mode skips prompts except a documented exception list: explicit ask rules, connector tools an organization set to ask, and MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction. Hook ask decisions are not on that list, so they carry no documented guarantee of surviving prompt-skipping modes, whereas content-scoped ask rules are additionally documented to force a prompt even for sandboxed commands in auto-allow mode.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the rule is evaluated by the harness before the matching Bash call and pauses it on a terminal prompt); what crosses the boundary is the human's confirmation or refusal rather than model output, and the tool call proceeds only after that approval
key.lifecycle: evaluated before every matching Bash call in the fixed deny, then ask, then allow order; the prompt fires even in bypassPermissions and sandbox auto-allow
key.failure_mode: The gate requires a human present: in headless -p runs nobody can answer the prompt, and in dontAsk mode the call is denied outright instead of prompted, so unattended pipelines stall or fail at the gate.

sheets.primary: An explicit ask permission rule, permissions.ask containing Bash(git push:*), placed in managed settings so no session can drop it. Step 2 changed my step 1 answer: I first chose a PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask", but the documented bypassPermissions carve-out names explicit ask rules, and hook decisions never override permission rules, so the rule is the mechanism that actually holds under every approval configuration.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook on Bash returning permissionDecision "ask". Rejected per the correction above: the mode-independent guarantee is documented for ask rules, hook approvals are subordinate to rules anyway, and a hook is one more thing that can fail to load.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code evaluates the ask rule before the Bash call regardless of permission mode, and the human at the terminal supplies the decision; the model cannot self-approve.
sheets.context_boundary: Evaluated inside the Claude Code process before the tool runs, and the prompt is rendered to the human in the terminal UI. Only the approval or denial outcome crosses back to the model, which never sees the rule text itself.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated on every Bash tool call for the whole session, in the fixed deny-then-ask-then-allow order, so it outranks the blanket allow configuration the team runs with. It stops applying only if the rule is removed from the settings scope that supplies it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed with respect to permission mode: it prompts even under bypassPermissions and even when a broader allow rule also matches. The residual gaps are string-shaped rather than mode-shaped, since a push reached through a wrapper script, a shell alias, an MCP git server tool or a subagent's own Bash call is not the literal git push text the rule matches.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on ask rules, and no plan restriction. The enabling-flag caveat is sandboxing: with the sandbox on and autoAllowBashIfSandboxed left at its default of true, sandboxed Bash runs without prompting for a bare Bash (or Bash(*)) ask rule, so the rule must stay scoped to Bash(git push:*) rather than the whole tool.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook matched on the Bash tool that parses the command string and, when it resolves to a push, returns a decision that forces a human confirmation (an ask decision where supported, otherwise a hard block whose reason tells the operator to perform the push themselves). Hooks run ahead of the tool regardless of the session's permission mode, which is what makes it survive the auto-approved configuration.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An ask entry in the permissions block of settings.json for the push pattern, rejected because the permission-mode configuration is exactly what has been turned off for speed, so a rule evaluated by that same layer is not guaranteed to survive it.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook decides before the command runs and the model cannot talk its way past a returned deny.
sheets.context_boundary: Matching runs in a separate process that sees only the tool input JSON. The decision and its reason string are what cross back into the model's context; the confirmation itself happens in the operator's terminal, outside the model's view.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated on every Bash tool call for the life of the session, and it stops applying if the hook entry is removed or if the push is performed through a surface that is not the Bash tool, such as an MCP git server.
sheets.failure_mode: String matching on a shell command is the weak point and it fails open under paraphrase: git -C elsewhere push, a push hidden behind an alias, a wrapper script, a compound command joined with && or ;, or a push triggered by a hook inside the repo all miss a naive pattern. It fails closed only if the matcher treats anything it cannot fully parse as a push candidate. In a headless or non-interactive run there is no human to confirm, so the safe behaviour there is outright denial rather than an indefinite wait.
sheets.version_caveat: The ask-style permission decision returned from a PreToolUse hook is the cleanest shape, but I cannot verify from model knowledge alone whether an ask decision is still honoured when the session is running with permission prompting bypassed. Until that is tested on the installed version, implement the rule as an explicit deny with an instructive reason, which is unambiguous in every mode.

sheets.primary: An explicit ask permission rule, permissions.ask containing "Bash(git push *)" (plus the PowerShell equivalent if that tool is in use), placed in managed settings so no local scope can drop it. An ask rule is the one construct that survives an auto-approved session, because bypassPermissions skips prompts except the ones an explicit ask rule forces.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask": it works, but it is weaker for this need, since hook wiring lives in settings a developer can edit and disableAllHooks removes every non-managed hook at once, whereas a managed ask rule cannot be overridden.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Permission rules are evaluated by Claude Code itself, ahead of and independently of any hook decision or prompt instruction.
sheets.context_boundary: Rule evaluation is harness-side and never enters the context window; what crosses the boundary is the prompt shown to the human and, afterwards, the allow or deny result returned to the model as the tool outcome.
sheets.lifecycle: It fires on every Bash tool call whose parsed command matches the pattern, in every session where that settings file is in scope, under any permission mode including bypassPermissions and auto, and stops only when the rule is removed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for what it matches, but Bash argument patterns are fragile and matching is the weak point: a push reached through a script, a Makefile target, an aliased wrapper, or a tool such as gh does not match "git push *", so the halt is silently skipped. Match each subcommand form you care about rather than trusting one pattern.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate applies to ask rules themselves. The relevant restriction is a mode one: bypassPermissions still honours explicit ask rules, so this is the documented way to keep one prompt alive in an otherwise auto-approved session, and a matching ask rule prompts even when a PreToolUse hook returned "allow".

sheets.primary: An ask rule, "Bash(git push *)" in permissions.ask, placed in managed settings (or project settings) so it loads regardless of session configuration, with a parallel "PowerShell(git push *)" entry where that tool is in use. Ask rules are evaluated before allow rules and are one of the few things that still force a prompt under bypassPermissions and auto mode.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask" for git push. It achieves the same prompt, but adds a script and a process spawn on every Bash call for something the permission system expresses in one line, and a hook's decision is merged with sibling hooks rather than being authoritative.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code raises the prompt itself; the model cannot answer it, argue past it, or mark it 'don't ask again'.
sheets.context_boundary: The prompt is raised in the user's terminal by Claude Code and the human's answer stays in the harness; the model sees only the resulting tool result (the push happened, or it was denied). The rule itself never enters the model's context, so no prompt injection can reason it away.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies to every matching Bash or PowerShell call for the life of every session that loads the settings file. It is never consumed: unlike an allow prompt it cannot be answered with 'Yes, don't ask again', so it fires every single time until the rule is removed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed in interactive sessions, but the guarantee is only as strong as the pattern. Claude Code checks each subcommand of a compound command and deny/ask rules match past leading environment assignments, yet a wrapper script, a git alias, or /usr/bin/git push sidesteps a literal 'git push *' pattern. In dontAsk mode there is no prompt to show so the call is denied instead, and in headless -p runs there is no human present to confirm at all.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on ask rules themselves. The mode interactions are the thing to verify: bypassPermissions and auto still honor content-scoped ask rules, sandboxing's autoAllowBashIfSandboxed substitution does not suppress them, and a PreToolUse hook returning "allow" cannot suppress them either, which is exactly why this holds under any approval configuration.
